A restless ridge

Hekla’s recorded story

Hekla is a ridge-shaped volcano with a fissure along its summit. Its eruptions have varied enormously—some began explosively, others produced long lava flows. Written records reach back to 1104, while layers in Icelandic soil preserve a much older story.

Explore the complete eruption history →
Before settlement

Layers in the earth

Large prehistoric eruptions left the Hekla-5, Hekla-4 and Hekla-3 tephra layers—time markers found far beyond the mountain.

1104–1846

Accounts and ash

The first recorded eruption in 1104 began a long written chronology of explosive openings, lava flows and difficult years for nearby farms.

1947–today

The monitored volcano

Six modern eruption episodes transformed what scientists know about Hekla and how quickly its warning signs may appear.

Field notes

A few things worth knowing

01

Not one simple cone

Hekla combines features of a central volcano and an eruptive fissure. The summit fissure is called Heklugjá.

02

A remarkable record

The Icelandic Meteorological Office describes Hekla as Iceland’s third most active volcanic system in historical time.

03

Watch the experts

Activity is assessed by scientists using seismic, deformation, and other data. Conditions can change quickly; official notices matter.
